claims.text: Surface composition variations are the primary governor of premelting and melting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The extent of surface segregation and chemical short-range ordering locally reduces cohesive energy.
Reduced local cohesive energy accelerates atomic mobility at the nanoparticle surface.
Accelerated surface atomic mobility triggers premelting at lower temperatures than in nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution.
Two HEA nanoparticle sets should be prepared with comparable size but contrasting surface segregation.
Controlled synthesis routes should be used to promote or suppress surface segregation.
In situ TEM heating and high-resolution EDS mapping can be combined to compare structural evolution and surface composition during melting.
Holding heating rate, environment, substrate support, and particle size constant isolates surface-composition effects.
Surface-segregated regions provide local sites of reduced cohesive energy.
Surface-segregated nanoparticles will exhibit an earlier onset of premelting than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
Surface-segregated nanoparticles will have a lower complete melting temperature than compositionally uniform nanoparticles.
The premelting-to-melting transition range will be broader in surface-segregated nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship should hold for HEA nanoparticles approximately 3–10 nm in size.
Premelting may occur tens to hundreds of degrees lower in segregated nanoparticles.
Prior evidence supports the qualitative relationship between segregation and reduced premelting or melting temperatures.
The temperature difference may depend on elemental combination, synthesis method, and nanoparticle size.
Similar premelting and melting behavior in segregated and uniform particles would falsify the proposed governing role of surface composition.
